title: The proposed State Department tour and Blues Alley
summary: Tommy Gwaltney contacted her about a tour that didn't happen; she praises Blues Alley and the Manassas festival.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Do you have any recollection about that State Department tour? Who was trying to organize it, or, at least your participation in it, where it would've gone and why it didn't occur?

I'm not sure. Tommy Gwaltney contacted me about it. I think Tommy was trying to get something together. He probably had been approached. I had appeared down in Washington at Blues Alley several times. And he probably wanted to submit this to the State Department. I have no -- in fact, I never knew what became of the idea. I only know that it didn't come through. There is a possibility that Fat Cat might've had something to do with it. You know, when Blues Alley first opened,

Tommy Gwaltney and
Tommy Gwaltney and Fat Cat and the mayor of Arlington, Virginia were the three owners of Blues Alley.
And so -- you know, Fat Cat might've had something to do with sitting up and arranging or making some kind of contact with that tour.
Does he still have an interest in that club?
No. I don't think he nor Tommy have an interest. They may have maybe a few residuals, but I don't think so. I think they sold out.
And I have no idea. It's been through several hands since that time.
But it was a very nice club. I mean, it still is. It's one of the nicest clubs in Washington.
It's an intimate room, and it's -- the decoration is very subdued. They bring in a lot of the jazz musicians and soloists.
I mean, Marian McPartland has been down there with her trio; Charlie Byrd in there.
Was that his home base in

No.
He had another club?
He had another club, yeah.
And Wild Bill Davis, Bobby Hackett. A lot of the guys go down -- they did go down and work as soloists with the local trio.
And it was a good place to work. I understand they've changed the policy now to maybe have some of the modern music in there, or whatever is current -- commercially, you know.
I don't know. In fact, I don't eve know who owns it. It's been through several hands, and I've worked with several different owners in the club. I really don't know.
I haven't been down there in a couple of years now. So I really don't know what's happening down there.
But -- most of the people that were on this album, have appeared at Blues Alley at one time or other.

And the Manassas jazz festival is a big once-a-year thing held in December. Fat Cat calls himself "the poor man's Richard Gibson," because of the Richard Gibson's jazz party in Denver held every year.
